I consider to be an unwarranted attack on a gentleman who was formerly a member cf this house, a man with whom I had the privilege of sitting in this chamber for many years, and who sat afterwards for five years later than I did. Mr. Vallance is a farmer. He was a homesteader. He was living in an area of the country affected by this legislation. He is a man probably as well acquainted with the work that is being undertaken as any man in the area who could be selected. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) professes great personal regard for him; one might say, "greater love hath no man" than he expressed for Mr. Yallance. But apparently there was some other reason why Mr. Vallance would not be a fit and proper person to occupy that position, and that reason was given by the leader of the opposition, because he stated that Mr. Vallance was really a partisan. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated this afternoon, there is no man in Saskatchewan who has been more independent than Mr. Vallance in stating his views on all questions, whether within or without the house.
But let us assume that the reason given by the leader of the opposition is why he thinks that Mr. Vallance should not be chairman. I ask the leader of the opposition this question, has he been informed during this year by people in the area which Mr. Vallance has endeavoured to serve that they have found him to be an active political partisan, or has he been doing the work that is entrusted to him? I have been over that area;
I have travelled hundreds of miles through that country, and I have yet to hear anyone make a suggestion that Mr. Vallance is playing politics in even the remotest way. On the other hand, I have heard from many that he is doing the job in the best way that it could be done. Is that the reason it has been suggested that he is not a suitable man for the work? Because a man sits in this 'house, is he thereby unfitted to occupy thereafter any position in the service of the government?
Let us look at the situation. I sat in this house with another gentleman, of whom I wish to say nothing but the most kindly things; he sat on the other side, and he was made deputy minister of Marine and Fisheries. I say nothing more than that.
Was he a fisherman?

I am not saying whether he was qualified or not qualified. I merely make that statement. During the last five years an hon. member occupied a seat on the Conservative side as a supporter of the leader of the opposition. Where is he to-day? If there is
one appointment in the service of the dominion whose incumbent should be above political partisanship, it is that of a member of the civil service commission. The man to whom I have referred is a member of that commission. I am not stating that he is fair or unfair. I merely say that he holds that position and that he is a former Conservative member of this house.
A few nights ago, when the estimates of one of the departments were brought down, the leader of the opposition saw fit to remark that there was one official who apparently was not very well known to his minister. At that time the Postmaster General's estimates were before the committee. Every hon. member saw that the assistant deputy postmaster general was seated in front of his minister, and I think those who have been here for a number of years will recognize that we had in the person of that official one of the ablest men in the public service of Canada. I want to ask who appointed the deputy postmaster general, another gentleman who sat in this house on the Conservative side during the last five years as a follower of the leader of the opposition. Is the post office service in Canada an important service? I suppose there is no hon. member who will deny that it is one of the most important services carried on in the dominion. More than that, I believe every hon. member and every person outside the house will agree that one cannot become, without a great deal of experience, an efficient servant in a very important branch of the service. Yet we find that a former Conservative member of this house was placed, without having had any previous experience, in the important position of deputy postmaster general.
I come now to the tariff board, which is supposed to be of some service to this country, and what do we find there ? Another gentleman who sat in this house when I was a member. If I were to refer to him as a political chameleon, I believe I should be pretty accurate. No man knew where he stood. He was all things to all men.
Until the vote came.

Until the vote came. If one goes over the records of this house and parliamentary guide, one can find, as far as I have been able to discover, no other instance where a man represented himself to be a Progressive and added the words, "previously Liberal." Everyone knows that the hon. gentleman never was a Liberal, and had it been known in his constituency that he had been a Conservative all the time, he could never have represented it in this house. To what position
Farm Rehabilitation Act

was he appointed? To the tariff board. I say to this government that if there is anything more ridiculous that I can think of than their keeping a man of that type on the tariff board, I do not know what it is.
I am inclined to think the leader of the opposition does not really like Liberals. Before this house organized itself, there were a number of members who sat here for many years, and some of them occupied very important positions. They were known to have taken part in public life, and the very first thing we had, something I regretted very much and I have no doubt the right hon. gentleman regrets it to-day, was a serious reflection on the hon. gentleman who is Speaker of the house. The same thing is true with regard to yourself, Mr. Chairman, and now we find it true of our friend Mr. Vallance. I am not saying some of the gentlemen appointed by the right hon. gentleman were not honourable men, but it ill becomes the leader of the opposition to single out Mr. Vallance and hold him up to scorn because he once happened to be a Liberal, when the right hon. gentleman himself, if it was a crime to make such an appointment, was guilty of the same thing time and again. The discussion this afternoon has been unfortunate in some respects, but there is only one hon. gentleman in this house who is responsible for initiating that discussion and that is the leader of the opposition.
Might we have repeated now the suggestions made by the Minister of Agriculture about two and a quarter hours ago? We ought to get back to the bill.

My suggestion was that we revert to section one of the bill, the new section 3 of the act, subsection one. I propose that it should read:
The governor in council may establish one or more advisory committees to be known as prairie farm rehabilitation committees, the members of which shall hold office during pleasure.
And the next subsection should read:
One of the members of each advisory committee shall be appointed chairman thereof by the minister.

Will there be one central committee? Will the chairman of the several advisory committees constitute a central committee? It seems to me it is important that there should be one committee responsible to the minister.

Yes. There will be one central committee, but it may not necessarily be exactly the same personnel as the present one. There are obvious reasons for that.
[Mr Young.]
That committee saw fit to agree to there being at least two other committees, one being a committee to deal with water and another to deal with re-grassing. We desire to have that sort of committee appointed in the same way as the central committee is appointed to act. There is another committee that has been in existence. On this committee the three western provinces are represented. Only one exception could be taken to the appointment, following the remarks made this afternoon, and that is that Mr. Vallance was chairman of that committee. The provincial governments of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan have each a representative on that committee, and that committee is a much smaller one and can be got together more easily than a committee spread all over Canada. If there is any objection at all, it can be only with regard to that one committee. I believe all the members of that committee are employees either of the dominion government or of one of the provincial governments. Mr. Charlesworth of Alberta, Mr. M'Gavin of Saskatchewan and Mr. Attwood of Manitoba I think are on that committee, and these men were all originally members of the staff of the Interior department at Ottawa. Mr. Vallance simply sits as chairman at meetings which are held for the purpose of discussing the activities of the committee.
Are these to be regional committees or will they have charge of various phases of the work? The minister mentioned the question of water, for example.

In checking the matter up since last evening and discussing it with officials who have been more closely connected with the administration than I am personally, I am informed that what was said a few moments ago by the leader of the opposition is correct, that so far as the voluntary committees in the country are concerned, no legislation is required, and we do not desire to have the authority to name the chairmen of these committees. They are named by the farmers themselves.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I take it that the amendment is that the word "advisory" shall be inserted before the word "committees" in the eighth and eleventh lines.

Listening to the amendment proposed by the minister, I suggest that all it accomplishes is to change the name of the committee. It makes no change in the principle of this section of the present bill as originally introduced1 by the minister. Does the minister agree with me?

Farm Rehabilitation Act

It changes it to this extent, that we cannot appoint an administrative committee under this section. I take it that one of the objections of the leader of the opposition was that we should not have administrative committees appointed in this way.

I listened with a good deal of interest to the minister this afternoon, and, when he finished, the situation seemed to me to be very much confused. One part of his argument seemed to me to prove that all that was being done under this act had been undertaken, was initiated, or was under way, and that this act was unnecessary to accomplish what was being done under it. He went away back into history, starting at the beginning, to tell what had been done by the provinces and the organizations they had set up, and in my opinion he minimized the value of this act. In fact, he almost led me to conclude that he ought to be asking for the repeal rather than for the amendment of the act.
This act was drafted with great care and a special advisory committee was set up. We have asked the minister on different occasions to give us the names of those who were appointed to this committee. We have not received that information and I repeat the request. On the other hand, when we make reference to the report of this advisory committee, we find that a great deal has been accomplished, that it has really done wonderfully well in the short time of its existence. The act was not passed until April, 1935. Evidently some things that were done in 1936 could not have been undertaken in 1935 owing to the lateness of the season-seeding and that sort of thing. Then again it was necessary to have the committee organized. All that had to be done in 1935. Really I think the committee has accomplished a very satisfactory result. Its activities were based upon this act and upon the provisions of the Supplementary Public Works Construction Act of 1935. So, on the whole, I think this committee of the whole must come to the inevitable conclusion that the results of the legislation have been very creditable, very satisfactory indeed. Then the question naturally arises, why make any change when so much has been accomplished by the machinery which has been set up. It is not suggested that two committees can do more than one. In fact, there is likely to be confusion, conflict and division of responsibility. Under the act as it at present exists, there is no difficulty in subdividing the
advisory committee by regulation or otherwise, and having the members undertake special studies of any particular subject. I should like the minister to give the names of those who are on the advisory committee.

Doctor E. S. Archibald, Ottawa, chairman. Dominion Department of Agriculture; James H. Girvin, Medora, Manitoba grain growing farmers; Olaf Nyland, Shaunavon, Sask., Saskatchewan grain growing farmers; P. C. Colquhoun, Maple Creek, Sask., Saskatchewan live stock farmers; Leonard Koole, Monarch, Alberta, Alberta grain growing farmers; R. P. Gilchrist, Wild Horse, Alberta, Alberta range farmers; Professor J. H. Ellis. Winnipeg, government of Manitoba; Dean A. M. Shaw, Saskatoon, government of Saskatchewan; 0. S. Longman, Edmonton, government of Alberta; E. W. Jones, Calgary, Canadian Pacific Railway Company; Doctor W. J. Black, Montreal, Canadian National Railways; F. J. Freer, Winnipeg, mortgage companies of Canada; Doctor E. S. Hopkins, Ottawa, Dominion Department of Agriculture; B. P. Alley, Toronto, Canadian Bankers' Association.
Mr. Alley was the only member of the advisory committee unable to be present. There were others present at the meeting, but those are the members of the committee.

I think the reading of that list of names is sufficient to convince the committee that it is a thoroughly representative, non-political, efficient and capable committee. I do not think the minister for a moment contends that he can improve upon the personnel or nature of the committee. He has given no good reason why this committee which has accomplished so much should be set aside. The minister says, " I may reappoint them." But why set them aside if he intends to reappoint them?

I think I stated more than once yesterday that I have no present intention of having any different central committee from the committee named. But there is the possibility that I may have to appoint someone else because of the wishes of some members of this committee, in view of the work which is to be done this spring.
Does the minister contend that under the legislation as it exists, he has not the power to fill any vacancy?

No, but I contend that this summer we may be doing something so related to some of these organizations as to make their representatives desire not to be on an advisory committee in connection with it.
Farm Rehabilitation Act
The minister is crossing a bridge long before he comes to it.
Oh, I shall come to it.

Yes, I think the minister is anxious to get to the bridge, but his statement indicates that he is setting out to cross it before he arrives. He suggests that possibly some of these men may not be willing to act, but surely it would be time enough-

Well, it may be the other way around; I may not wish them to act. I am sure if those conditions arose, they would not wish to act. The railway companies still have considerable interest in lands all over that country; the banks have an interest in lands all over that country, and so have the loan companies. Surely it is not contended that if we should be dealing with the resettlement of people on lands in which the banks and railways and loan companies have an interest, their representative should be on the advisory committee in connection with those activities. There is the possibility that we may not wish them to be on it, and the possibility that they would not wish to be on it. We wish to have power to change if we desire.
The minister has it now. Can the minister suggest any gentleman more capable of giving good advice than say Doctor W. J. Black-
No.

-who is familiar with the development and has long been associated with settlement work. Surely the magnitude of the interests of these corporations justifies their being represented on the committee. And the basis upon which I take it other members are appointed to this committee is that they are interested in and affected by the work of the committee. Why should not the railways and the mortgage companies, which have a very substantial interest, be represented on the committee in common with those who have equal interests and must be just as much concerned in the proper development of that part of Canada as any citizens? They have a special interest and a general interest.

There is no objection to any of these men individually. For such work as I have been speaking of, there would, I think, be no desire whatever on the part of either the individuals concerned or myself for any change. But if we do start the kind of work I outlined a moment ago, I think both those organizations and the department would desire to have a different type of advisory

committee. We might want to have represented on that committee the municipal organizations, if we are going to ask such organizations to cooperate with us. If dealing with lands which really belong to the people named here, I think it would be advisable to have on the committee, say the representatives of the municipalities rather than the representatives of these companies. We would be sitting around a common table discussing what we are going to do; when we get to a certain point we may want to discuss the matter with the advisory committee, and you have on the committee the same individuals as you have represented in your discussions. That condition might easily arise under the arrangement in the present act.

I want to come back to the question I raised with the minister before in respect to the proposed amendment. He pointed out that his amendment would have the effect of confining the activities of the committee to be appointed to those of an advisory nature. I sent for the act, and I direct the attention of the minister to section 7, which provides that:
The governor in council may make such regulations as may be necessary or expedient for effectual execution and working of this act and the attainment of the intention and objects thereof.
That is a very broad omnibus section which, I submit, would entitle the government, by order in council, to vest in the committee any power which it desired within the ambit of the statute. Merely changing the name of the committee by inserting the word "advisory" will not accomplish the purpose which he ostensibly desires to accomplish, and which he says he desires because of a defect in the amending statute, as pointed out originally by the leader of the opposition.

Of course, there is section 5, which pretty well takes care of what the hon. member has in mind. It states:
No member of the committee shall receive any payment or emolument for his services, but he shall be repaid all actual reasonable travelling or other expenses in connection with the work of the committee.
No, no; I have not anything of that kind in mind. I have in mind what the minister said he wanted to accomplish.
This is not my suggestion, at all.

May I make myself clear, because I think the minister misunderstands me. I shall try to do it briefly. The minister proposed an amendment to the bill-

Farm. Rehabilitation Act
No, I did not; it is proposed from the other side of the house, and I am trying to amend the bill to suit them.
Oh, no; that is not what I proposed, at all.

I shall have to go over the subject in greater detail. Yesterday the leader of the official opposition suggested to the minister that his bill, now before the committee, should be constructed and worded so as to accomplish a certain purpose. The purpose was that the committees to be appointed should be limited to being advisory committees. To-day the minister says he will do this by amending the name of the committees, by calling them "advisory committees." The point I am trying to make is that the amendment will not accomplish the purpose the minister himself says he desires to accomplish, in order to meet the point raised by the leader of the opposition.
I do not believe section 5 touches the point at all. I am not considering whether they can or can not be paid, or whether or not they receive travelling expenses. That is not the point. The point is this: Is it to be limited to an advisory committee, or is it to be a committee not limited to act in that capacity? I do not think the amendment accomplishes the purpose.
As I understand the discussion, advisory committees would be committees which we could call together from time to time, and from which we would get advice on policies we may have under consideration.
Yes.

The principle of the bill as I understand it, as it was originally provided and finally became law, is that no member of the committee shall receive payment or emolument. I believe the intention was to get the type of individual who would give service of this kind without consideration. If the act is amended, as now suggested, and the committees are all made advisory committees, then each of them would be of that nature. That is the only change I see which would be made by adding the word. That is, we would be compelled to appoint men who would not receive pay for their positions, and would be called in merely for the purpose of giving advice.
Section 7 reads:
The governor in council may make such regulations as may be necessary or expedient for the effectual execution and working of this act and the attainment of the intention and objects thereof.
That would apply to all the actual administration under the act. Under the act as it was originally passed, we are not bound even by the advice we get from these committees.

The minister, in the statement he has just made, has supported the very contention I am making. He said the regulations they could pass under section 7 would deal with the administration of the act. All right. Now that, he says, is something which he does not want the committees to have power to do, namely to perform administrative functions. He wants them limited to being merely advisory.
No, not-

And I say that because
section 7 gives power by order in council to confer upon them administrative functions, he is not accomplishing the purpose his amendment is intended to accomplish. That is the only point I am trying to make.

I would prefer to have
the bill as I introduced it yesterday. I do not think it has the weaknesses which have been pointed out. But in order to try to meet those who have been criticizing, I am prepared to insert the word "advisory," and to confine those sections of the act to an advisory committee. I do not think anyone would suggest that we could carry on the whole administration of the act under a committee of that kind, and ask them to do all the work in connection with it. The proviso would have to be in any act. I do not know how we would proceed if we took out section 7 and made the whole thing advisory. I do not see any difficulty about leaving section 7 in, and having these advisory committees to call in at any time so that we may discuss with them whether or not we are proceeding in the right direction.

I am not suggesting that
the minister should take out section 7. I wish merely to put myself clearly on record to the effect that the amendment now proposed by the minister will not accomplish the purpose he would like to accomplish to please this side of the house, or to please anybody. I feel it my duty to call that to his attention.

If the minister will be
good enough to look at his initial statement, he will observe that he said he desired to provide for the appointment of committees, other than advisory committees.

Yes, but my right hon.
friend-
Farm Rehabilitation Act
That is what the minister said.
But my right hon. friend has been trying ever since to convince me that that was wrong. Is he now going to condemn me for changing my mind on it, after three or four days of discussion?

I pointed out that section 7 was employed for that purpose, namely to appoint administrative committees, because section 7 provides for the appointment of committees to administer the act. This afternoon the minister takes that view, but he suggests that I was anxious to support the appointment of another advisory committee.
No.

That is not my intention, at all. I would only have to point out that if the word "advisory" is put before the word "committee," it does not follow my suggestion. The effect of it would be to give a provincial bent to the operation of the committee, because if you are going to have more than one committee they may not agree on their advice. The whole theory was for one advisory committee, and to call all other committees you may like under section 7. The effect of the bill is to repeal section 3. It states, precisely:
Section 3 of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, chapter 23 of the statutes of 1935, is repealed, and the following substituted therefor.
That is the position. The minister states he is trying to meet our views, but I am sure he is mistaken as to that because I never have suggested at any time that there should be two advisory committees.

I would not suggest that I am going so far as to cut it down to one committee, but I am prepared to make all committees advisory in the sense that the first one was advisory, and to have it controlled by the fact that we cannot pay them emoluments of office.

The difficulty I pointed out yesterday was that if you have more than one advisory committee your advice may not be the same. You have too much advice, because you have advice from several committees.
If I had been permitted this afternoon to read from the files I could have cleaned up that point. One of the first things the committee did was to recommend that two other committees be appointed.

The minister is quite within his rights to read the minutes of the meeting. The fact that they are on the file has nothing to do with it; they are supposed to be somewhere else. But he should read the minutes of the meeting, if he so desires.

The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 18, to amend' the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act-Mr. Gardiner- Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 2-Duties of committees.
Do I understand that this clause is amended to read, "The advisory committees shall consider and advise"? Is that what is proposed?
That is the intention, yes.

I can only say that that does something which I did not contemplate would- be done, and which I hardly think anyone contemplated being done. This creates more than one committee of the same kind which may or may not give similar advice with respect to the problems to be considered. This creates a situation which I do not think the minister had in his mind and which I certainly did1 not have in mine Will the word "advisory" be added before the word "committees" in the last line?
It will be added in each line where the word "committees" appears.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 3-Committees.
Is there an amendment to this section?

On section 4

Appropriations.

I think the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition in connection with section 4 is that it should read in this way:
The governor in council may from time to time authorize the expenditure in each of the fiscal years from and including 1937-38, up to and including the fiscal year 1939-40 for the purposes of this act, such sum or sums as may be appropriated by parliament in each of the said fiscal years respectively, for said purposes.
That is, the words "from time to time" are to be added after the word "may" in the first line.

I am not quite sure that is the way in which the minister would desire to have it. I would think the proper phrasing would be:
The governor in council may from time to time authorize the expenditure for the purposes of this act in each of the fiscal years

That is, the expenditure would be authorized for the purposes of the act.
There is no objection to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman's amendment is intended to make plain the normal procedure in such cases.

Yes, quite. While the amendment is being prepared, I should like to make one observation with respect to the statements made to this committee this afternoon by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) with reference to a member of the tariff board. Mr. Campbell came into this house in 1921 as a supporter of the present Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). Mr. Campbell was then a Progressive and continued as such, so far as I know. I mention this merely because the records in the journals of the house do not indicate what has been said here. I understand the Minister of Mines and Resources is regarded as a Liberal and Mr. Campbell came into this house in 1921 as one of his ardent supporters and continued as such, so far as I know, until he was appointed to the position which he now occupies.
I may say that the attack which was made upon the deputy postmaster general could have been made with equal force upon the
late Sir Wilfrid Laurier who appointed Doctor Coulter to the position of deputy postmaster ganeral. Doctor Coulter was regarded' as being a most efficient officer, although the same conditions as those to which reference has been made prevailed at that time.
So far as the civil service commission is concerned, it consists of three members and not one. I do not think the party predilections of the member who was appointed need be dwelt upon too strongly in the light of his speeches during the time he was in parliament. It was because he possessed certain academic qualifications and a certain independence of mind that it was thought he would make an admirable appointee, a belief which I think is shared by all who have any knowledge of the operations of the commission. In any event, this is not similar to the case which I was discussing, as would be apparent on the face of it.
I regret greatly the observations made with respect to the Speaker, but if similar circumstances arose again, as a matter of public duty I would have regretfully to follow the same course as I then pursued. I have no sorrow or regret for having done what public duty necessitated my doing on that occasion.

Mr. Chairman, I am not quite sure what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is trying to prove with respect to Mr. Campbell, now a member of the tariff board. If I did not make myself clear this afternoon. I should like to make another attempt this evening. Mr. Campbell came into this house as a Progressive from a constituency which had never elected a Tory. In the parliamentary guide it will be found that he states he was a Progressive and he then adds something that no other member of this house has ever added, namely, that he was previously a Liberal. Those of us who sat in this house during those thin years when we had not the majority we have to-day, have no doubt as to what his politics were when it came down bo a close vote. No one knows that better than the leader of the opposition.
I dispute that and the journals show quite the opposite.
If the right hon. leader of the opposition does not know that, I think he is the only member who does not.
What has all this to do with the dry areas?

I was not in the house in 1921.
Farm Rehabilitation Act

Further, Mr. Campbell was never opposed by a Tory at any time. With regard bo the deputy postmaster general, may I say that I merely called attention to the fact that he had' been a Conservative member of this house during the last parliament. Mr. Sullivan was appointed to a position which, in my judgment, calls for training in a particular work. I have yet to find one man either in or outside this house, unless it be the leader of the opposition, who approves that appointment. If the right hon. gentleman wants to know what the members of the Post Office Department from coast to coast think about it, he could make the same inquiries as he dad about my friend Mr. Vallanee.
I want to say one thing more about Mr. Vallanee. I do not think I made any objection to the leader of the opposition attacking Liberals. He is well known for doing that at all times. But had he shown us that Mr. Vallanee had been inefficient in his duty since being appointed; had he shown that he had been partisan in the performance of his duty since his appointment, then I could see some purpose in the right hon. gentleman's reference to this gentleman. As I listened, Mr. Chairman, I could not help recalling the saying about "Satan rebuking sin," and if there is one hon. gentleman in this house who should not bring up such matters it is the right hon. leader of the opposition.
What about the hon. member himself?

Mr. Chairman, I am going to make just one observation in reply. I was not discussing Mr. Vallanee except to point out the effect on public opinion of such an appointment, in view of the fact that his predecessor was the manager of the demonstration farm at Swift Current and was doing this work as part of his ordinary duties. This position now carries S4.000 per year, which, compared with the salary paid to Doctor Archibald, gives some indication of what the general situation is.

I understand that the minister is going to set up a number of committees. I should like to ask him to what extent the expenses of these committees will prevent them from reaching the proposed objective. Of course, certain sums of money will be devoted by parliament for certain projects, and these committees will entail a certain amount of expenditure. Would the minister give us some estimate of what that will be?

The original committee met only twice, and the expenses were for railway fares to the point of meeting and hotel expenses. The expenses, I imagine, would be very small, but I believe these committees will be called oftener if set up in the way we suggest. The expenses might be a little more, although in all probability they would not, because the distance the members would have to travel would be much less.

Mr. Chairman, I was going to wait until the amendment was put, but as the discussion may get off on another tangent there are one or two things I should like to say now. First, I should like to associate myself with those who complimented the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) yesterday upon his presentation. I felt, however, that perhaps the financial commitments for which money would have to be appropriated by parliament had not been sufficiently emphasized in his presentation. I believe that the problem which we face in western Canada is much greater than most of even the members of the House of Commons realize, and that it will entail the expenditure of a great deal more money than many expect.
I have in my hand a copy of the report which was made by those who conducted the soil survey in the province of Saskatchewan, and to which reference has frequently been made since this legislation was introduced. They state, and quite accurately, that even a casual view of the land situation in western Canada will show that not all the land settled is fit for the plough. The minister made that very clear yesterday.
I should also like to put before the house, and on record, the classification that is made in this soil survey of the lands largely in the area to which the minister referred yesterday, although this area takes in a little more land as the line runs horizontally through Prince Albert and then south to the international boundary. The surveyors divide the soil into six groups, and give the percentages in each area. They classify as superior soil 7T per cent of that area, and included in that superior soil area is the district which I have the honour to represent and the district around Regina, Melfort and one or two other areas. The next classification is: (2) Very good, 5-9 per cent; (3) moderately good, 16-9 per cent; (4) fair, 25-4 per cent. The point I am making is this, that fair land, and land better than fair amount to 55-3 per cent of that area, while land that is poor or very poor amounts to 44-7 per cent of the area. Of course, not all that poor land or very poor land is settled, but a great deal of it is.

Farm Rehabilitation Act
I am going to ask the minister what responsibility the department is going to assume for the continuance of these soil surveys and for making the chemical analysis which I think ought to be made, because, as all of us who come from this area know, you cannot say that any particular area is all bad, since there are variations within any given area.
I am disturbed, too, by the fact that a number of new settlers have gone into the north country and settled on land which is deficient in certain chemical constituents. There is that deficient whitish soil, for instance, that we see in that north country. It seems to me that we have to face this problem in a larger way than we are inclined to do at the present time.
There is one other table which I should like to place before the committee, and that is a summary of the surveys made of farm income on this land, with its varying types of soil. According to the farm management *department of the university of Saskatchewan, a farmer on the superior soil operating a half section of land could have in an average year a net income of between $307 and $516, and on a section a net income of from $1,280 to $1,588. On the moderately good soil his income would range from as low as $4 on a half section to as high as $262, and on a section from $547 to $859. On the poor soils at the end of the year the farmer would find himself with a net loss of $10 on a half section and an income of $523 on a section. But on the very poor soils the farmer simply cannot live on a half section.
Are those figures after all living expenses, clothing, food, and so forth, and wages are taken out?
No, not wages.
Wages for his help?

No, not wages for hired help, and not wages for any member of the family, but the figures include living expenses, which run roughly-I have not the exact figures before me-from seven to eight hundred dollars a year, according to the locality.
Did not the hon. member say that it was net income?

This is net income after living expenses only have been taken out. There is no allowance in these figures for interest, no allowance for wages for the family
or for the hired man, and nothing for replacements. I think these figures will be found in bulletin No. 64 of the university of Saskatchewan.
Is it not presupposed that the family is large enough to require no hired help?

I would not say that, but it is anticipated that the farmer would be able to get along with the help he had around him; that is true. On the other hand, I am pointing out that nothing is allowed for wages for that family, and the living expenses figure out at about $700 or $800 a year, as the case may be.
May I ask the hon. member whether these figures represent an average over a period of years or are they for one year?
A period of years.
For what period?
I think the surveys were made at different periods.
I think it was ten years.

I believe that 1910 to 1914 was taken as the basic period and-the minister can correct me if I am wrong-that 76 cents per bushel for No. 1 Northern on the farm was the basis of the wheat price that the university used.
Seventy-seven cents.

Seventy-seven cents.
Thank you. Seventy-seven cents was the basic farm price of wheat. What I am pointing out is that on poorer lands the farmers cannot make a living, and something will have to be done in order to enable them to make that living.
The other afternoon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) mentioned the success achieved at the Matador ranch. That ranch happens to be in my constituency, and it is performing a very useful function for the farmers of that locality. But let me point this out, that the Matador ranch has not been broken up. It still retains the original prairie sod, and many of the lands which we have been discussing and are stating might be used for pasturage in the future, will take a long time-
Farm Rehabilitation Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Much of the Matador has no sod at all. I have been over it many times.
The minister is quite right. Quite a bit of it is stony.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And sandy.

And sandy, yes. I think it requires about forty-six acres to maintain a single animal on that piece of land. Nevertheless the ranch performs a very useful service to the community. In the rehabilitation of much of this land the problem will be to grow grass again, and in my opinion that will take a considerable length of time. It may come naturally, by the weeds holding the soil together and forming something of a cover for the growth of grass later. But the point I am making is this, that I think this committee Should support the minister in any reasonable request he may make for funds for this particular purpose. I do not believe the condition can be exaggerated, and unless we are prepared to rehabilitate this area, the entire economic life of this dominion will suffer. As was said the other afternoon, it is not a local but a national problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, just a word with respect to the use of figures which are so discouraging as those quoted by the hon. member. Without at all disputing their accuracy in portraying what they purport to portray, I am always a little doubtful about the value of such generalizations as they represent. I might illustrate by saying that the soil report to which my hon. friend referred, and referred quite properly and accurately, relates to all of the area in Saskatchewan south of Prince Albert. May I suggest to him and to any practical farmer in the house that what is poor land in northeastern Saskatchewan, will have, by reason of the extra rainfall which that part of the province gets, a greater productive capacity than very good land in a district which does not receive sufficient rainfall.
And lower evaporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And the advantage of lower evaporation. It happens that my farm is shown on this soil survey map as consisting to almost half its extent of what would be called good land, and of almost half of only very fair to poor land. I know that the poor land on my farm, were it located in southwestern Saskatchewan, by reason of the difference in the rainfall would not produce what

it produces in the Yorkton district of Saskatchewan. It is just an illustration I am endeavouring to give of how easy it is to go-wrong when basing one's ideas upon the necessarily rather broad generalizations of an examination of that kind. I think the same may be said with respect to the economic survey. We all are familiar with farmers in poor districts who have good incomes, and we are all familiar with farmers in good districts who have poor incomes. We must allow for the wide variation in the human factor. Personally I am one of those who-believe that while governments can cooperate, as we are now proposing still further to cooperate, in the solution of these problems,, the real working out of them will be based upon the intelligent application by the individual farmer on his own farm of the-information which is made available to him either through this source or through the agricultural colleges or other scientific institutions which are working on the problem. More of our western problems have been solved during the last forty years by intelligent work by individual farmers on their own farms, the knowledge of which work gradually extends through the community and by and by throughout the whole west,, than by any other means. I take it that this rehabilitation proposal in so far as it relates to that phase of -the problem is intended to-make available the practical knowledge to the greatest possible number of farmers in order that they may work out their problems intelligent!}' on their own farms. And may I say that I know of no better man as the active head of that sort of work than a practical farmer like John Vallance, who knows the men, who knows the soil, who knows the conditions, and who is in the work with his whole heart.

I agree absolutely with what the Minister of Finance has said, and I do not take issue with what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said, because he did not have in front of him the document about which he was speaking. I have in my hand the document issued by the department of farm management for Saskatchewan, covering a survey of several years. The years 1910 to 1914 were taken as the base years for price. In central Saskatchewan the average price of No. 2 northern wheat during the five years was about 77 cents per bushel. But in referring to the figures on income and otherwise of farms, I do not think it would be fair to let the impression go out to members of

Farm Rehabilitation Act
this chamber or to other parts of Canada that this is a hopeless proposition, because everything depends upon weather conditions in this territory and economic conditions elsewhere.
Table 1A. which is the first table given in the management book, refers to inferior prairie soil, and the figures provided therein are cash figures. Farm living expenses in cash are allowed on behalf of the farmer and his family for groceries, meat, light and fuel, furnishings, clothing, health and miscellaneous, a total of 8708. Everyone knows that on any farm in Canada

I think I am safe in saying on any- many items are available for living purposes that do not have to be paid for or accounted for in cash. But these are farm living expenses in cash on one-half section lands, chiefly sandy and gravelly, with rolling topography, and subject to frequent loss of crops, particularly from drought. These are the poorest lands dealt with, and the sort of lands, I take it, as to which the minister would like to see a change in the location of the farmers living on them. These lands would not carry any principal or capital debt at all on the crops that the farmers were getting at the price I mentioned. In addition to the farmers' living expenses, paid in cash or allowed for, farm expenses in cash cover items such as the following: machinery repairs; gas and oil and grease; blacksmithing; building repairs, 1 per cent of value; paint and painting; fences new and repairs; small hardware; fire insurance; threshing; twine; telephone; breeding fees; taxes and miscellaneous expenses. No car expenses, but horse expenses have been provided for conveyance, and no labour expenses have been provided because these costs are on a basis of a family of four adults to the half section farm and it was not considered that on a farm of that type much hired help would be needed outside threshing.
The same type of land on a section farm would carry a debt, amortized in a period of twenty years, at six per cent, of 83,062, which would amount to S10.07 per acre of crop land or $4.78 on land per acre over the whole of the section. It is not anticipated that on land of this kind a very large percentage will be under cultivation, and that is why its debt carrying capacity is so low.
Coming to the next type of land, mixed soils with " burn-outs " or clay spots frequent, and on which wheat production is generally problematical, after allowing for living . expenses totalling $708 and farm expenses, cash, amounting to $348, we find there is a
deficit in the cash requirements. But even on a section farm there would be a deficit. This is poor soil. Taking average prairie soil, mixed textured soils, principally loams, undulating to rolling, with varying amounts of stones, sloughs and waste, and subject to considerable variation in crop yields, we find an allowance of $719 for farm living expenses, cash, and $4S9 for farm expenses in cash, leaving a net cash income of $228, and a net income of $42, after taking into account many charges in addition to those I have given. This land would carry a principal debt of $482 per half section, according to this calculation. On a section of such land, however, because of the larger income and the relatively lower expenses the debt capable of being amortized in twenty years at six per cent would be $8,086.
As we get into the better lands, though still very much in the drought area, fair to good southern park lands, we find that on a half section, using these figures as the basis of calculation, there could be carried a principal debt of $1,208 amortized in twenty years at six per cent, and on a section of such land it is calculated that a principal debt of $9,130 could be carried. In all the section farm figures there is provision for labour, but on the half section farms there is not.
As regards fair to good eastern park lands, average northern park lands, mixed textured soils, and silty clay loams, moderately free from obstructions, producing high yields of wheat and other crops, and heavy clay land which is the choicest wheat land of Saskatchewan, the figures are all set out in this pamphlet. But even on the poorest types of land, according to this survey, in reasonable years under reasonable weather conditions and at prices we regard as very moderate-77 cents for No. 2 northern wheat-there was at that time a possibility of the average farmer having $700 to spend in living expenses in addition to what he took off the farm in kind, besides maintaining machinery, buildings and so on.
It is well known that much land has been settled which should not have been settled had we known then what we know now, and I am satisfied that it is one of the objects of the rehabilitation board, as the minister said the other day, to get some of this land out of cultivation. The area under the plough in many of these lands was small in comparison with the total area of the farm, and on the poorer lands there is a possibility, indeed a probability, that many farmers would not have a half section but a section. As men have moved away, naturally more land is left
Farm Rehabilitation Act

to be divided among those remaining, and where land will not carry a heavy capital debt or, in some cases, any debt at all, it is comparatively easy for those who remain in the district either to obtain ownership of the land surrounding them and now vacant, or, if they cannot get the ownership, to get the use of it.
I would say one word about the poorer white clay soils of northern Saskatchewan. I know they are not so good in some respects as the lands around them. But they are not as poor as a stranger might imagine by looking at them. They have been under bush for a long time and snow and water have lain there much longer than on the surrounding lands, with the result that more of the mineral content has leached out. But if I were to tell the committee that in northeastern Saskatchewan some of these white clay lands produced last year cash incomes of around $100 an acre, the statement might be received with some incredulity, or I might be asked to give further explanation. The explanation is simple. It may be that these lands will not produce heavy crops of wheat or coarse grains, but they are suitable for alfalfa, which is now grown to a considerable extent in northeastern Saskatchewan. The farmers there began growing this crop only a few years ago and last year the yield was from 400 to 800 pounds per acre and sometimes more than that. At 23 cents per pound for No. 1 registered seed, with two cents allowance for handling by the cooperative selling agency, leaving a balance of 21 cents net, it will be seen that a crop yield of four, five, six, or seven hundred pounds and sometimes more than that makes it possible to secure $100 per acre income off these alfalfa lands. I do not say that this would cover the acreage of these farms, because not many acres are yet under cultivation. But it is probable that in that section are the best alfalfa seed lands to be found on this continent. How long that will continue I do not know. Many of the lands that have been under cultivation for some time and that are being put under cultivation now have not always been used to the best advantage. New uses are to be found for them, and I commend this to the attention of the rehabilitation board. I suggest that they should pay particular attention to getting these lands under some type of crop, whether grass or grain or legume, that will be more suitable to the land itself, to the climatic conditions and to the other needs of the district. I believe the rehabilitation board can do important work in that regard. Experiments have been going on for a good many

years with crested wheat grass. The former Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) began using crested wheat grass in an effort to-restore prairie soil and before his time his predecessor the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Tolmie) was engaged in similar work.
Let me say one last word. In my opinion the rehabilitation board might well devote some time and money to trying out seeds from other parts of the world which seeds have been found to be successful under conditions at least as unfavourable as we have in western Canada. There are parts of northern Russia and Siberia, possibly in South America and high Asia, that have made possible a reasonably prosperous type of agriculture. The Department of Agriculture of the United States has been importing some of these seed grasses, legumes and other farm products for many years, but much of the work they have done has been lost because these things have been pigeonholed. Every once in a while some new scientist, on the principle that a new broom sweeps clean, takes the packages out of these pigeonholes and makes use of them. Crested wheat grass was introduced in the United States forty years before it was tried out in Canada.
I might mention something I saw last year. I saw trucks coming from Minot, North Dakota, running day and night, hauling seed of crested wheat grass, sweet clover and alfalfa and other seeds from northern Saskatchewan back to the Dakotas and probably Montana where crested wheat grass had been left lying idle for so long.

I quite agree with the hon. member for Melfort in his description of the district he represents. The figures I was using were for the poorer types of land, and speaking from memory I think he pretty well substantiated the figures I used. I think it is true that we in western Canada have in days gone by drawn a picture which was a bit optimistic, and at present perhaps we are inclined to be too pessimistic. We have to try to strike a happy mean. But it is of no use, however, closing our eyes to the tremendous difficulties facing the Department of Agriculture in the southern part of the province. In the northeast it is a different story on account of the rainfall, but in the southwest and the extreme south the outline given of conditions by the hon. member and myself is, I think, substantially correct. If one looks over the income tax returns which were quoted yesterday, it will be seen, for example, that for the year 1932-33 only thirty-two

Farm Rehabilitation Act
Saskatchewan farmers paid income tax; in the following year twenty-nine; the next year, thirty-eight, and last year, ninety-six. That gives a pretty fair picture of conditions. The same thing is shown by the number of lapsed life insurance policies. The point I am trying to make is that this is a big problem, and any expenditures made by this government will be approved by the people of western Canada.

Having listened to the debate to-day, I have been wondering whether there is any province in western Canada but Saskatchewan. We must remember that either east or west of Saskatchewan there is a province with practically the same conditions existing. So I ask that those two provinces be not forgotten. While I do not agree with the minister in everything he says and does, I have to compliment him very highly upon the comprehensive and able report which he gave on this matter yesterday. I do not think anyone could make a much better job of it, and if he goes through to the end as he has started I think members of all parties will praise and congratulate him and the government of which he is a member.
I do not live in the dry belt, but a considerable portion of Battle River constituency is in that belt. So far we in the northern end of the constituency have been fortunate enough to have a little moisture. Last year our average crop in the northern end ran eight or nine bushels of wheat and ten bushels of oats to the acre. That, as hon. members will admit, is not very high, and even with good prices farming is not a paying venture. And this, I may say, is a pretty high estimate for the average in the northern part of the constituency, while in the southern part I know of thousands of acres where a binder has not been taken this year. In other parts they got one or two bushels, and where I live we got around eight bushels. Several problems have to be dealt with there. One is the feed situation during the winter. In the early part of the winter we felt that matters were going to be all right because we had a late open fall. But since then the west has experienced a lot of cold, and heavy snowfalls. This has brought about a serious condition for those who are short of feed, which means practically everyone in that dried-out district. How to put in a crop in the spring is one of their problems now, and I wonder whether it is not possible under this scheme to supply fuel oil so that tractors may be used instead of horses. I make this
suggestion so that the minister, following the good start he has made, may consider it. I am not making it for myself; I was lucky enough-if I may put it in that way-to have enough frozen grain in 1935 stacked up to carry me over last year too. Otherwise, as far as oats are concerned, I would be in exactly the same position as those in the southern part of the constituency.

Following the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), in which he said that we have perhaps been too optimistic in the past and now are getting pessimistic, I should like to say the same is true as far as what is known as the drought area is concerned. I think many people in Canada, and probably many members of the committee, have not a proper idea of that section of the country. There is plenty of good land in that area, although much land has been settled there which should not have been settled1 for grain growing. The governments of this country were responsible for that. But in that part known as the drought area we must remember that there has been settlement for only a short time, and that many people who went there to settle went with very little capital.	Some	of them were	not farmers.When they first settled in there, they were able to break only a very small part of their land, on which they had a good crop at that time. The next year they would have a little more broken, and again they had a good crop. They went on breaking more and more of their land, and people who were selling lumber for buildings, selling machinery and all those things that farmers there needed, believing that	it was a good	part' of	thecountry, allowed considerable credit to the fanners	there.	These farmers	went on	tobreak up their whole farm and put up buildings and buy machinery on credit, and then a drought period hit them before they had a chance to take a good crop off the whole farm or a large proportion of it. Had they been able to get a good crop on a large acreage for some years prior to the drought period they would have been able to come through	some	bad years, perhaps not	six
years, but the larger part of it, without a great deal of help from the government. The government has tried to help these people through this time of stress.
Conditions will not always be what they have been recently in that part of the country. There have been droughts there before, extending over a period of five or six years,
Farm Rehabilitation Act

but that was at a time when that part was not settled, and' therefore no one was greatly hurt by it. But if the people on the good lands in the drought area are held there and assisted by the government under this rehabilitation scheme to carry on, they will no doubt come to a period in which there will be sufficient rainfall, and with sufficient rainfall, that portion called the drought area will produce large yields of grain of the very best quality. If these people are helped1 through this period, we shall probably find that ten years from now in that part of the country they will be producing many, many millions of dollars worth of purchasing power for the benefit of eastern as well as western Canada. We shall find that although we have spent a considerable sum of money in endeavouring to help the people in that part of the country, the dominion as a whole will be well repaid for the money spent.

I have sat patiently for
two days listening to the discussion of the rehabilitation measure. Fortunately or unfortunately, as the case may be, I happen to be the representative of a large portion of the district which has been under discussion, and in which the rehabilitation plan is working.
About thirty years ago as a young man I went into the district, at a time when the early settlers were coming in. At that time I remember the criticism of the old timer was that the federal government of that day had allowed such a great portion of the land to be settled by farmers. I remember, too, that the then provincial member for the constituency of Maple Creek, known in those days as Fighting Joe Wiley, did make representations to the federal government in which he pointed out that a mistake was being made in permitting the settlement of large areas in the southwest section of the country.
Possibly at this time it might be well to give a bird's-eye view of what our southwestern country looks like. As the minister so ably pointed out yesterday,, the southwest is a plains area down the centre of which is a row of hills extending from the Rocky mountains, in an easterly direction. These are known as the Cypress hills, and to a certain extent they are wooded. In the hills there are numerous small lakes and springs which are the sources of creeks and small rivers. These are being rapidly developed as irrigation projects by the water conservation and rehabilitation committee.
Irrigation is not unknown in the great southwest. For more than thirty years there have been small privately owned and operated irrigation plants. Just south of the old town of Maple Creek, which is so well known in the southwest, is a rancher who has had irrigation over his land for a number of years. In 1936, despite the dryness of the season, he had 200 acres of alfalfa under irrigation, and from that land he cut 750 tons of good alfalfa hay. I maintain that in the development of our irrigation projects in the southwest, if we do nothing more than make sure that we supply our ranchers, stock growers and small farmers with a supply of fodder sufficient to carry their cattle over the winter, the expenditure would be warranted.
Yesterday an hon. member from Alberta asked the Minister of Agriculture a question regarding feed. In the last ten days I have received several letters and telegrams from southwest Saskatchewan on this subject. I have discussed the matter with the Minister of Agriculture, and he informs me that everything possible is being done to have feed shipped into that area. If each year we have to spend millions of dollars in shipping feed to that part of the country in order to keep the farmers' and ranchers' live stock through the winter, would it not be better business to spend an equal amount of money each year in the development of the great irrigation projects out there waiting to be developed. If people in eastern Canada would visit our great southwest and see the great developments which could be opened up, there would be no question about the house spending the the required amount of money each >
ear.

POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT Post Office-Outside Service
Salaries and allowances, $16,713,338.50.
Mail services, including mail services by air, $14,520,000.
Miscellaneous, including $5,000 to provide for payment of compassionate allowances to employees injured while in the performance of their duties or to other persons injured while performing duties in any way connected with the postal service or in protecting His Majesty's
fMr. J. G. Ross.]

Supply-Post Office
mails, or to the dependents of such employees or other persons who may be killed while so engaged, payments to be made only on the specific authority of the governor in council, $1,004,600.

I notice a large number of items appearing under this item, and I assume they are all under discussion. May I call the attention of the minister to the very unsatisfactory method of engaging rural mail carriers. It is well known that mail carriers in the cities and towns are paid salaries, and that the civil service commission make the appointments, selecting from the applications they receive those which, in their judgment, are the most suitable. I can never understand why in the country men are allowed to bid against each other, and why invariably the contract is given to the lowest bidder. In that way we get the man who places the lowest value upon his own labour. In these days, when a great many people are bard up, men are bidding against each other for these jobs until the point has been reached where bids are made away below proper values. I know of one rural mail route seven miles long now being operated for 87 cents per trip. I know of another one where $1,000 was being paid for a route twenty-two miles long. It was put up at auction some time ago and bid down for $480. Men cannot live on such wages.
Our government is making investigations into certain industrial plants, showing that great profits have been made and small wages paid, I do not think there is a more flagrant example of underpayment of officials than is to be found in the Post Office Department in connection with the rural mail carriers. There should be a minimum rate per mile for these rural mail routes. I admit that it may cost less to operate routes which lie along highways or in sections of the country where the roads are kept free of snow and where there are very good roads than it does to operate routes where the snow is not cleared and where the roads are not in good condition even during the summer time. I do not think any rural mail carrier in Canada should be asked to supply a horse and buggy and harness or a car for the delivery of mail at less than $50 a mile per year.
Does the hon. member mean the round trip?

Yes, on the round trip. I know of instances where men have not
been able to buy feed for their horses and keep them in condition to do this work. Quite often this job is looked upon as a sort of side line. I asked one man the other day why he had taken the contract at the rate he had and he told me that he was hard up, that he had had poor crops and was able to put a boy just out of school on the route where he could earn a little. These conditions should not exist and it is manifestly unfair to treat the rural mail carriers any differently from the carriers in the towns and cities. The men delivering mail are performing a very important duty in the community and they should receive at least a reasonable compensation.

Mr. Chairman, the matter that my hon. friend has brought up is not new by any means. It has been discussed, for some years and was discussed' at considerable length the other evening. I do not think I can add1 anything to what I said at that time. I assure him that I have as much sympathy for the rural mail carriers as has he or any other member of this committee. For years the law has been that contracts for over $200 shall be let by public tender after having been advertised. I do not know how any man can complain when he gets a contract at the rate at which he tendered for it. As I mentioned the other evening, there have been very few contracts let in the time that I have had something to do with the Post Office Department, without at least half a dozen men, either by correspondence or by requests through their members, seeking to obtain the contract at the same rate at which the lowest tenderer obtained it.
The hon. member speaks of $50 per mile, but that would1 be very much in excess of the present rate. Just the other day I had a most interesting interview with some representatives of the rural mail carriers' association. Some hon. members also attended that meeting. These men, all mail carriers, were a very fine type. Nearly all had been engaged in some other occupation before becoming rural carriers, some of them having been in two or three different occupations. Some of them had started out carrying mail by filling out a contract taken by someone else. In not one case that I know of has the contract holder been anxious to throw up his contract and go back to the job he had previously.

Supply-Post Office

I say to my hon. friend, what I do not think I need to say to him, that for the past few years the men whose mail has been carried by these carriers have been working on their farms for less money, or at least not much more money than the carriers received. No doubt some of these mail carriers are fulfilling their contract at very low rates, but they have not been in nearly the unhappy position of some of the farmers to whom they are delivering mail. I am not attempting to say that we are paying the price which I think will be paid1 when times improve, because conditions always change when times get better. As farmers are able to make more on their farms, fewer of them will tender for these mail routes. Perhaps that condition will bring the remedy which, after all, would be the best remedy.
My hon. friend is too good a business man to argue for one moment that one could fix a minimum price which would be fair all over Canada. This is a country of varying climates and conditions. In some parts of it there is very little snow and that for only a short period of the year, while in other parts there is very deep snow for much longer periods. The only solution would be to attempt to fix a minimum rate for each district, and that would be almost impossible to do. I agree with what my hon. friend has said with regard to these men working for lower wages than are received in the cities, but the remedy which he suggests of a minimum price per mile would bring up the very question to which other hon. members would object, namely, to whom would the contract be given when half a dozen bid the minimum price?
Mr. THOMPSON The civil service commission.

It would be quite interesting to see the civil service commission sitting in Ottawa deciding as to who would get a route up in northern Alberta or away down in the county of Essex. I have nothing more to say. I do not think the plan my hon. friend suggests is at all feasible because there is as much difference between the various miles that a rural mail carrier travels as there is between the horses that cover the ground. There are no two miles the same, and each man, when 'he is tendering, has to judge for himself what price he considers will be of advantage to him if he should be so fortunate as to have his tender accepted.

I cannot agree with what the minister says, and I think I made that clear when I said that each route should be judged on its own merits. I said that the cost of delivering the mail would not be as much on some roads as on others, for instance, on a highway that is kept ploughed in the winter time.
I can remember quite well when rural mail delivery was first started. When an application was made, a man was sent out from the department to go over the route before it was decided to start the service. I remember our good friend Mr. Coolican coming out to Almonte, and I drove him with a horse and buggy over the first rural mail route that was let. He examined the route very thoroughly, and I say that it would be quite easy to have every rural mail route examined and a price set for that route.
The minister also stated that the men could not be appointed by the civil service commission. I want to say that the appointments are made now right here in Ottawa. The applications are sent in here; the department decides who is to get the route, and it would be just as easy for t'he civil service commission to make the appointment. The lowest tenderer almost always gets the contract.
No, no.

I have never yet known a mail route where the lowest tenderer did not get the contract. The appointment is made from Ottawa, and the department give the contract to the lowest tenderer. It would be just as easy for the civil service commission to do this, and I think these appointments should be made by the commission. I am not in favour of patronage, and I do not approve the manner in which these appointments are made now. I know that in the five years from 1930 to 1935, when the government I supported was in office, I was written to in every case when a rural mail contract expired, and asked whether I would recommend that it be renewed or new tenders invited. I shall tell the committee what I did. In those five years I never put one route up for tender. I did not care who the man was who had the contract, so long as he was doing his duty. I renewed them all because I am not in favour of a man putting up a mail route for tender simply because the present man on the route voted against him. I always felt that if the man was doing his duty and was being a good

Supply-Post Office
public servant, he had no right to be interfered with. But under the present system these men are at the mercy of the man who holds the patronage for the riding.
No.
My hon. friend is entirely wrong.

I am not asked about these rural routes any more, but my opponent
is, and he has stated that he has been tormented about them. He makes recommendations to the department that the same man have his contract renewed or that the route be put up for tender, but he has no say as to who shall get the route if opened up, because the department gives it to the lowest tenderer. He has the say as to whether the man who is already performing the service shall have his contract renewed. I think this is a very unsatisfactory state of affairs. I say that $50 per mile even as a minimum would not be too much to pay for delivering mail on many of our country roads, and it would be quite easy to have each route considered on its merits.

As the minister has said, this is a matter which has been before parliament for a number of years. The subject comes up almost every year. I agree that the ideal way would be to pay the men on a salary basis, but as the minister has pointed out, there are great difficulties in arranging that. It has also been suggested that we follow the United States system, where the postman is given a uniform and so much per mile per year for carrying the mail. This is, of course, something that we may look forward to having some day in Canada.
The last speaker (Mr. Thompson) brought to the attention of the committee a matter on which I had intended to say something, and that was the question of patronage. I noticed that when he made his statement about patronage, we heard "No, no" from a number of hon. gentlemen opposite, but I know that at present, some weeks before a contract is about to expire, a notice is sent to the member of parliament supporting the government or to the defeated candidate supporting the government. I received these levters myself for five years, and I have in my hand a copy of a letter which I have taken from my file, and which I think it would be just as well to put on record. The form is a long one. It winds up with No. 37. The letter is headed "Post Office Department, Canada," and there is a line for the date.
The letter reads:

Re,-

Now listen to this:
The department considers the rate paid as reasonable and is prepared to renew the contract.
I should be glad of your advice as to whether it would be in the public interest to allow this service to remain with the present contractor, whose name is given, or whether you consider it would be in the interest of the department to invite tenders for a new contract.
